"You're up again," Hemant said, finding his wife Jyoti on the balcony.
"I did everything right. No phone in bed, same wake-up time, no tea after lunch. And I'm still staring at the ceiling."
"How long has this been going on?"
"Weeks. And it's not just the sleep. Everything feels grey. I cried on the metro yesterday over nothing."
"Jyo, that's not something to push through alone."
"I keep thinking I should just try harder."
"You have tried hard. Maybe it's time to see Dr Sen. Not instead of your routine, alongside it."
"What if she says it's nothing?"
"Then we'll know. And if it's something, we'll know that too."
Jyoti leaned against him. "Okay. I'll call the clinic in the morning."
"I'll come with you."

passage: Last winter I thought I could fix my sleep like a spreadsheet. Blackout curtains, the same alarm every morning, no screens in bed, a warm drink. For weeks I lay awake anyway, my mind looping over work and my dad's retirement money. I started dreading bedtime. My friend Simran listened on a video call and said quietly, "Sabina, you've done all the right things. This is the point where you tell a doctor." I was embarrassed, as if needing help meant failing. But I booked an appointment. The doctor asked about my mood as well as my nights, and we made a plan together. I kept the curtains and the steady alarm; they turned out to be part of it. Looking back, the brave thing wasn't pushing through. It was asking.

qa.a: Simran likely felt concerned and wanted Sabina to stop battling alone, which is why the advice was gentle but clear.

Supervisor's note, 12 March
Jyoti has looked worn out for about six weeks. Today she told me she lies awake most nights, even though she has cut screens at night, kept a fixed wake time and darkened her room. She said she has started dreading bedtime and feels low most mornings. Her plan was to "just push through till the project ends". I told her, gently, that this sounded like something a doctor should hear about, not something to push through. She booked an appointment with her doctor for Friday, and I've cleared her afternoon so she can go. She asked me not to share details with the team, and I won't. I'll ask how she is next week, without pressing.
Sumit

Night 23 of this. 2:10 am.
I've done everything the articles say. Same wake-up at 6:30, even on Sundays. Phone in the kitchen. Blackout curtains. Warm milk. And still I lie here with my heart going fast, making lists of everything that could go wrong at work.
Vidya called tonight and asked how I was. I said fine. She said, "You've said 'fine' in that voice for weeks." Then I cried on the phone for ten minutes, which probably answers it.
She made me promise to book a doctor tomorrow and not wait and see. I've stuck a note on the mirror: CALL CLINIC 9 AM. I'll keep the habits too; Vidya says they'll help with whatever the doctor suggests.
I feel stupid needing help with sleep. But three weeks of this isn't stupid. It's just too long.
Aditi

passage: For five weeks Maria, the young English teacher at the school in Kumta, had lain awake till two. She had tried everything: warm milk, no phone after nine, the same wake time, a dark room with the fan on. Still she stared at the ceiling, and in the daytime a heavy worry sat on her chest. She didn't want to make a fuss. Her landlady, Ganga, found her crying over a stack of corrections. 'Enough, child. This is not something to push through alone.' The next morning Ganga went with her to the doctor at the taluk hospital. Maria kept her steady wake time and dark room, and began talking about the worry too.

qa.q: Where did Ganga go with Maria?
qa.a: To the doctor at the taluk hospital.

qa.q: Why hadn't Maria sought help sooner?
qa.a: She felt reluctant to make a fuss and kept trying to push through, even while worry sat heavy on her chest.

qa.q: Why was seeing a doctor the wise next step?
qa.a: Weeks of poor sleep with daytime worry had not eased with good habits, so a doctor could help alongside her routine.

qa.a: Ganga probably felt worried and protective, deciding Maria shouldn't face it alone.
